content.overview: The promisee may get the work done by a third party after notice and recover the cost. That choice bars later specific performance.
content.study: Give the enacted notice. Keep the invoices. Do not ask for 10 after you have used 20.

learningObjectives: Explain substituted performance under the post-2018 Section 20.
Apply the statutory written-notice period and recovery mechanism.
Distinguish substituted performance from specific performance and compensation.
enhancement.definition: Section 20 allows the party suffering breach to obtain substituted performance through a third party or its own agency and recover actually incurred expenses and costs, subject to the statutory conditions.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Substituted performance is an option following breach. It requires the statutory written notice of not less than thirty days and, once the contract is performed through the statutory mechanism, the claimant cannot also seek specific performance against the party in breach.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 20(1)–(4), read with Sections 14(a), 16(a) and the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
essentialIngredients: A contract must be broken because of non-performance.
The suffering party must give written notice of not less than thirty days calling for performance within the specified time.
After refusal or failure, substituted performance may be obtained through a third party or the party's own agency.
Recovery is limited to expenses and costs actually incurred, spent or suffered as provided by Section 20.
After substituted performance, specific performance cannot be claimed; compensation remains separately claimable under Section 20(4).
enhancement.detailedExplanation: The amended Section 20 creates a practical substitute for waiting for the defaulting party to perform. Notice is a statutory precondition: the suffering party must give written notice of at least thirty days. If the breach continues, the work may be completed through a third party or the claimant's own agency. The claimant may recover the statutory costs, but once this route is taken, Section 20(3) bars a later claim for specific performance against the defaulting party. Compensation remains available under sub-section (4).
examples: A contractor fails to complete a promised installation. The employer gives the required written notice allowing at least thirty days for performance. After continued failure, the employer engages another contractor and seeks recovery of the qualifying expenses under Section 20.
enhancement.distinctions: Section 20 is substituted performance; Section 16(a) treats obtaining substituted performance as a personal bar to later specific performance; Section 14(a) also excludes contracts where substituted performance has been obtained.
enhancement.problemApplication: A party has a broken contract and wants another contractor to complete the work. Identify the breach, verify the written notice period, document actual costs, and determine whether the party has elected a route that bars later specific performance.
examAnswerStructure: Identify the breach and contractual obligation.
State Section 20 and its notice requirement.
Analyse substituted performance and recoverable costs.
Address the bar on later specific performance.
Conclude on compensation and other available relief.
keyTakeaways: At least thirty days' written notice is required before substituted performance under Section 20(2).
Substituted performance prevents a later claim for specific performance against the party in breach.
Compensation may still be claimed under Section 20(4).
